item.title: Joint tenants and rent repayment orders – watch our webinar with Justin Bates KC
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

A recent Upper Tribunal ruling has clarified important rights for joint tenants seeking rent repayment orders against landlords who fail to meet legal requirements. The case of Ebony Brown & Ors v Nyack Semelo-Shaw [2026] has established that individual tenants can pursue claims without needing all co-tenants to join the application.

Understanding Rent Repayment Orders

Rent repayment orders require landlords to return some or all rent payments when they've committed specific offences. Common grounds include operating unlicensed Houses in Multiple Occupation (HMOs) or properties covered by selective licensing schemes without the required permissions. The tribunal must be convinced "beyond reasonable doubt" of the landlord's wrongdoing before granting such orders.

Previously, tenants faced difficulties when the First-tier Tribunal insisted on collective applications from all joint tenants. The recent Upper Tribunal decision overturned this approach, confirming that individual tenants can claim back:

  • The specific rent amounts they personally paid
  • Their share of rent even if paid through another tenant
  • Repayments without requiring participation from all co-tenants

Implications for Joint Tenancies

The ruling provides much-needed clarity for shared households where tenants might have different circumstances or willingness to challenge their landlord. Legal experts highlight several important considerations following this judgment:

  • The Renters Rights Act 2025 extended liability to superior landlords for offences committed from 1 May 2026
  • Tenants may wish to seek professional advice about their specific situation
  • Documentation proving individual rent payments could strengthen any claim
  • Previous cases about tenancy continuity when sharers change remain relevant

For those interested in the legal details, Justin Bates KC, who represented the successful tenants, discussed the case and broader tenancy issues in a recent webinar. The session covered practical aspects of joint tenancies and when tenants might be treated individually rather than collectively.

This development marks an important step in protecting tenants' rights, particularly in shared accommodation where licensing requirements often apply. Renters in similar situations might consider reviewing their position and keeping thorough records of all payments made.

item.title: Nationwide launches 1% deposit mortgage
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Nationwide Building Society has introduced a groundbreaking mortgage product allowing first-time buyers to purchase a home with just a 1% deposit. The "Helping Hand 1% Deposit Mortgage" could enable eligible borrowers to secure properties with deposits as low as £2,352 on an average £235,200 first home, dramatically reducing the savings period compared to traditional 5% deposit requirements.

How the 1% deposit mortgage works

This innovative product forms part of Nationwide's existing Helping Hand range, which has already assisted over 85,000 first-time buyers since its 2021 launch. Key features include:

  • Minimum deposit requirement of just 1% of the property value
  • Borrowing potential of up to six times the applicant's income
  • Exclusive to five-year fixed-rate deals at 5.99% with no product fee
  • Available only on existing residential properties (not new builds)
  • Minimum income thresholds of £30,000 for single applicants or £50,000 for joint applications

Nationwide estimates the scheme could help more than 5,000 additional buyers annually, with £1 billion earmarked for lending through this product each year. The society reports that less than 0.1% of its existing Helping Hand mortgages are currently in significant arrears, suggesting responsible lending practices remain in place despite the lower deposit requirement.

Potential impact on first-time buyers

The new mortgage could substantially reduce the time needed to save for a home purchase. Analysis shows that someone saving 5% of average monthly net income could accumulate a 1% deposit in approximately 15 months, compared to nearly six years for a 5% deposit on the same property.

Henry Jordan, Nationwide's Group Director of Mortgages, commented: "First-time buyers face challenges from both deposit requirements and borrowing limits. Our new product helps level the playing field, particularly for those without family financial support."

Industry experts have welcomed the initiative, with Rachel Springall of Moneyfacts noting: "This offer comes at a crucial time for the housing market. Extending Helping Hand to include 99% loan-to-value mortgages could make homeownership achievable for many more people."

Prospective borrowers should note that all applications remain subject to standard affordability checks and credit scoring. While the lower deposit threshold improves accessibility, applicants will still need to demonstrate they can comfortably meet monthly repayments at current interest rates.

item.title: First-Tier Tribunals slash landlord rental rises by nearly half
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

New research reveals that whilst most landlords are securing rent increases through First-Tier Tribunals, the approved rises fall significantly short of initial requests. Analysis by lettings platform Goodlord shows tribunals have granted 61% of landlords' Section 13 notices since May, but with notable reductions to proposed hikes.

Substantial gap between requested and approved rises

The data indicates landlords have typically sought 9.8% rent increases, yet tribunals have approved an average rise of just 5.8% - representing a 40% reduction from initial proposals. Only one in three landlords (128 cases) received their full requested increase. Some extreme cases highlight the tribunal's role in moderating rent adjustments. In a striking London example, a landlord's proposed 445% increase (from £550 to £3,000 monthly) was reduced to a still-substantial 264% rise (£2,000), following consideration of local market rates and property conditions.

Tenants securing notable reductions

Approximately 38% of cases have resulted in favourable outcomes for tenants. In Manchester, one renter successfully challenged a proposed increase from £1,650 to £1,700, with the tribunal instead reducing the rent to £1,450 monthly - a 12% decrease from the original amount. The tribunal referenced comparable local properties to justify this decision.

Potential system pressures emerging

Goodlord CEO William Reeve warns the current caseload may represent "the tip of the iceberg", expressing concerns about the tribunal system's capacity. He notes: "The tribunal is a valuable new resource for tenants, but private rental sector professionals are rightly anxious about potential overwhelm." The ease of lodging appeals through digital platforms, coupled with the automatic rent freeze during proceedings, may encourage more tenants to challenge increases as a standard practice. This could create a cycle where landlords factor potential appeals into initial requests, potentially exacerbating the volume of cases.

With tribunals taking an average of 22 weeks to process cases, the current system faces challenges in maintaining timely resolutions. Both landlords and tenants may wish to consider these dynamics when approaching rent negotiations, particularly in areas with significant rental market pressures.

item.title: Two-thirds of homeowners considering an interest-only mortgage
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

New research reveals that nearly two-thirds of recent homebuyers would contemplate switching to interest-only mortgages to cope with rising borrowing costs. The study highlights growing financial pressures as homeowners face significantly higher repayments when remortgaging in today's elevated interest rate environment.

Mortgage payment concerns mount

Estate agency Benham and Reeves surveyed 910 homeowners who purchased properties within the last five years, finding that 73% expressed worries about increased mortgage costs when their current deals end. Only 18% of respondents knew precisely how much their payments might rise, while 38% hadn't yet investigated the potential impact.

The research illustrates how dramatically repayment costs have changed. A homeowner who secured a five-year fixed-rate mortgage in October 2021 could see monthly payments jump from around £733 to £1,039 when refinancing today - a £306 increase. Just 9% of those surveyed said they could comfortably manage such a rise, while 54% would need to adjust household budgets and 37% would struggle to afford it.

Interest-only mortgages as a temporary solution

Faced with these financial pressures, 64% of respondents said they would consider switching to interest-only repayments. In the example case, this could reduce monthly payments from £1,039 to £670 - a potential saving of £369 per month or £4,428 annually. However, borrowers should note this approach doesn't reduce the outstanding mortgage balance.

Among those contemplating interest-only arrangements, 71% planned to return to repayment mortgages when financially possible, while 13% would wait until interest rates fall. Concerningly, 14% admitted they hadn't considered how they would eventually repay the capital.

Marc von Grundherr of Benham and Reeves commented: "While interest-only payments can provide breathing space, they aren't without risks. Homeowners need a clear repayment strategy to avoid compromising their long-term financial security."

Mortgage holders approaching the end of their current deals may wish to seek professional advice well in advance to explore all available options. Lenders typically require robust repayment plans when approving interest-only mortgages, and borrowers should carefully consider both short-term affordability and long-term financial implications before making any changes to their mortgage arrangements.

item.title: Another bank turns to the bank of mum and dad
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

HSBC has become the latest lender to introduce a mortgage product designed to help first-time buyers by incorporating family support into affordability calculations. The bank's new Joint Support Mortgage allows relatives to boost a borrower's application through their income, without requiring any ownership stake in the property.

How the Joint Support Mortgage works

This joint borrower sole proprietor arrangement enables a family member (such as a parent) to have their income considered alongside the main applicant's earnings. Key features include:

  • The property remains in the sole name of the primary borrower
  • The supporting family member must obtain independent legal advice
  • The main applicant must earn at least £20,000 annually
  • Both parties are jointly responsible for mortgage repayments

HSBC's product launch coincides with research revealing strong parental willingness to assist with home purchases. The survey found 77% of parents consider helping their children onto the property ladder important, while 88% would contemplate some form of financial support.

The growing role of family assistance

With property prices remaining high relative to wages, family-assisted mortgages are becoming an increasingly common solution. HSBC's data suggests 41% of parents with adult children at home prioritise their offspring's financial goals equally with their own.

Oli O'Donoghue, HSBC UK's head of mortgages and savings, commented: "Our Joint Support Mortgage provides a practical way for relatives to help increase borrowing potential without property ownership complications. We ensure all responsibilities are clearly understood from the outset."

Prospective borrowers might weigh this option against alternatives like guarantor mortgages or gifted deposits. As with any significant financial commitment, seeking independent advice could help determine the most suitable approach for individual circumstances.

item.title: Rent arrears can top £9k by court hearing
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

New research highlights the growing financial strain on landlords as rental arrears frequently balloon to over £9,000 before reaching court hearings. The study by LegalforLandlords reveals how delayed possession proceedings allow tenant debts to accumulate dramatically, with London cases averaging above £14,000 in unpaid rent by the time disputes reach resolution.

Why rental arrears escalate during legal processes

Landlords facing non-payment of rent often encounter substantial delays in regaining possession of their properties. The typical timeline from first missed payment to court hearing spans several months, during which:

  • Tenants continue occupying the property without payment
  • Legal costs and court fees begin accumulating
  • Landlord insurance policies may require formal proceedings before paying out

In many regions outside London, the research indicates arrears commonly double from initial amounts to exceed £9,000. The capital's higher rental values push this figure significantly higher, creating particular challenges for property investors with mortgages to service.

Protective measures for landlords

While landlords cannot eliminate all risks, several strategies might help mitigate potential losses:

  • Conducting thorough tenant referencing before agreeing tenancies
  • Considering rent guarantee insurance products
  • Acting promptly at the first sign of payment issues
  • Maintaining contingency funds to cover mortgage payments during voids

The research underscores how the combination of high rents and procedural delays can create substantial financial exposure. Landlords with buy-to-let mortgages may wish to review their risk management approaches, particularly in high-value rental markets where arrears escalate fastest.

With court backlogs continuing to affect possession cases, the findings highlight the importance of preventative measures in residential lettings. Both new and experienced landlords might benefit from reassessing their tenant selection criteria and protection strategies in the current climate.

item.title: £561bn potential for brownfield sites
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

New research has uncovered substantial potential for housing development on brownfield sites across England, with London standing out as a prime location for regeneration. Analysis suggests these underutilised urban spaces could accommodate 1.45 million new homes, representing a total property value of £561 billion.

Brownfield sites offer housing solution

The UK Planning Database (UKPD) findings highlight how previously developed land could play a crucial role in addressing England's housing shortage. Brownfield sites – which include former industrial areas, disused railway yards and abandoned commercial premises – present opportunities for regeneration without encroaching on green belt land.

With many local authorities facing pressure to meet housing targets, these findings may influence future planning decisions. Homeowners and property investors might consider monitoring brownfield development plans in their areas, as such projects could potentially enhance local property values and infrastructure.

London leads brownfield potential

London emerges as the region with the greatest brownfield potential, accounting for a significant portion of both the housing capacity and property value identified in the research. The capital's abundance of disused industrial sites and underdeveloped urban spaces makes it particularly suited to large-scale regeneration projects.

For those considering property investment, areas with approved brownfield development plans may be worth watching. Such regeneration often brings improved transport links, new amenities and employment opportunities, which could make surrounding properties more attractive to buyers and renters in the medium to long term.

While brownfield development typically involves higher initial costs than greenfield projects – due to factors like land remediation – the environmental benefits and existing infrastructure connections often make these sites appealing to developers and local authorities alike.

The substantial figures revealed by this research suggest brownfield regeneration will likely remain a key part of England's housing strategy. As planning policies continue to evolve, these underused urban spaces could transform into vibrant new communities while helping to preserve the countryside from excessive development.

item.title: Edinburgh’s postcode hotspots
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
Edinburgh's Property Market: Postcodes With the Widest Price Variations

By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Recent analysis of Edinburgh's property market reveals striking differences in affordability between postcodes, with some areas commanding premium prices whilst others remain relatively accessible to first-time buyers. The latest ESPC data highlights how location continues to play a pivotal role in determining property values across the Scottish capital.

Prime Locations Command Premium Prices

The most expensive postcodes in Edinburgh typically cluster around the city's historic centre and sought-after suburban enclaves. Areas such as EH3, encompassing the West End and parts of the New Town, consistently top the charts for average property values. These locations offer proximity to premium amenities, prestigious schools and Georgian architecture that attracts both domestic and international buyers.

Other high-value postcodes include EH10 (Morningside and Bruntsfield) and EH4 (Stockbridge and The Grange), where period properties and vibrant local communities sustain strong demand. Homeowners considering these areas may need to account for significantly higher deposits and stricter affordability checks when mortgage planning.

More Affordable Alternatives Within the Capital

At the other end of the spectrum, several postcodes present more accessible entry points to Edinburgh's property market. EH6, covering Leith and its surrounding areas, has seen substantial regeneration in recent years whilst maintaining relatively lower average prices. Similarly, EH11 (Wester Hailes) and EH17 (Craigmillar) offer potential for buyers seeking value within the city boundaries.

First-time buyers might consider these emerging neighbourhoods, where government schemes like Help to Buy Scotland could make homeownership more attainable. However, it's worth noting that even in these more affordable areas, property prices have generally risen in line with Edinburgh's overall market trends.

Factors Influencing Price Variations

The disparity between Edinburgh's most and least expensive postcodes stems from multiple factors:

  • Proximity to top-rated schools and green spaces
  • Transport links and commuting times to the city centre
  • Architectural character and property types available
  • Local amenities and community facilities
  • Regeneration projects and future development plans

For those researching Edinburgh's property market, comparing postcode-level data could help identify areas that align with both budget and lifestyle preferences. Mortgage applicants may find it beneficial to consult with independent financial advisers to understand how different locations might affect their borrowing options.

As Edinburgh's property landscape continues to evolve, keeping abreast of postcode-level trends remains crucial for both prospective buyers and investors. The city's mix of historic charm and modern development ensures diverse options, though careful financial planning is essential when navigating its varied price points.

item.title: Christmas rental rates revealed
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

Festive season rental prices across the UK have risen by 4% compared to last year, according to the latest market analysis. The Cotswolds has claimed the title of the priciest short-term let destination during the Christmas period, with many popular rural retreats and market towns seeing significant demand from holidaymakers.

Seasonal rental market trends

Data from property analysts shows a steady increase in short-term rental costs during the December period, continuing a trend observed in recent years. The 4% year-on-year rise reflects growing demand for seasonal lets, with many homeowners choosing to rent out their properties during the festive break.

Several factors appear to be driving this trend:

  • Increased popularity of 'staycation' holidays
  • Growing demand for rural and scenic locations
  • Families seeking larger properties for multi-generational gatherings
  • Work-from-home flexibility allowing longer seasonal stays

Regional variations in pricing

The Cotswolds has emerged as the most expensive area for Christmas rentals, with its picturesque villages and proximity to London making it particularly desirable. item.title: Buying UK Property as a Non-Resident: Mortgages, Tax and Costs in 2026
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Purchasing UK property as an overseas buyer presents unique challenges, from navigating mortgage options to understanding tax implications. With London transactions taking nearly six months on average to complete in 2026, international investors may need to factor in extended timelines alongside financial considerations.

Mortgage Options for Non-Resident Buyers

Non-UK residents typically find fewer mortgage products available compared to domestic buyers. Many high street lenders restrict their offerings, though specialist providers often cater to international investors. Borrowers might consider:

  • Expat mortgages for UK nationals living abroad
  • International buyer products from private banks
  • Limited company structures for portfolio investors

Lenders generally require larger deposits from non-residents, often starting at 25-30% of the property value. Interest rates may also be higher than standard residential products, reflecting the perceived additional risk.

Tax Considerations for Overseas Investors

UK property purchases trigger several tax obligations that non-residents should understand:

  • Stamp Duty Land Tax (SDLT) with a 2% surcharge for non-resident buyers
  • Capital Gains Tax on property sales, now applying to all non-UK residents
  • Income Tax on rental profits if letting the property
  • Inheritance Tax implications for properties held in personal names

The tax treatment varies depending on the buyer's circumstances and whether the property is held individually or through a company structure. Professional tax advice is often essential for international investors.

Additional Costs and Timeframes

Recent data shows London property transactions averaging 174 days from offer acceptance to completion - significantly longer than other UK regions. Overseas buyers may wish to account for:

  • Currency exchange fluctuations during extended completion periods
  • Additional legal fees for cross-border transactions
  • Potential costs for property management services
  • Higher insurance premiums for unoccupied properties

Working with solicitors experienced in international transactions could help streamline the process and avoid unnecessary delays.

While UK property remains attractive to global investors, the combination of financial, legal and logistical factors means thorough preparation is crucial. Seeking specialist mortgage and legal advice early in the process may help non-resident buyers navigate the complexities of the UK market.

item.title: Double council tax removing second homes in some areas
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Recent government data reveals England has seen a significant reduction in second home ownership, with approximately 20,000 fewer properties classed as secondary residences compared to 2024 figures. The decline appears most pronounced in coastal areas where councils have implemented double council tax charges on second homes, with these locations experiencing both steeper property price drops and faster rental growth than the national average.

Double council tax impact on property markets

Analysis of council tax records and Land Registry data shows second home numbers fell by 9.7% in the year to September 2026 across 30 local authorities charging premium rates, compared to just 2.6% elsewhere in England (excluding London). These same areas have witnessed the most substantial house price corrections since the 2022 market peak, with values declining 6.6% versus a 1.2% dip across other regions.

The effect proves particularly stark in nine council areas where second homes represent over 3% of housing stock. Locations including Cornwall, North Devon, the Isle of Wight and the Isles of Scilly have seen average prices fall 8.8% from their peak - nearly triple the 3.0% decline recorded across the rest of England. This translates to approximately £27,000 off a typical £280,000 property in these sought-after coastal destinations.

Diverging trends for buyers and renters

While prospective purchasers benefit from improved affordability in these areas, tenants face growing pressures. Private rents in the nine highlighted districts have surged 21% since late 2022, only slightly below England's 25% average increase. This rental growth continues despite the cooling sales market, reflecting strong demand for holiday lets and limited long-term rental supply.

The analysis reveals a clear geographical pattern: councils with higher proportions of second homes subject to doubled council tax charges show more pronounced price declines. In areas where fewer than 0.5% of properties attract the premium, values remain 1.1% above 2022 levels. Coastal regions demonstrate particularly marked variations, with prices down 9.2% where 3%+ homes pay double tax, compared to 3.0% falls where under 1.5% do.

North Devon leads the downturn with values 14.0% below peak, followed by other popular second home destinations that saw exceptional pandemic-era price growth now partially reversing. For homeowners in these areas, the changing market dynamics may warrant reviewing property strategies, whilst prospective buyers could find improved purchasing opportunities in previously overheated locations.

item.title: Landlords seek data protection clarity on rental register
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Landlords across England are seeking urgent clarity on data protection measures as the government prepares to launch its new private rented sector register. With the phased rollout beginning on 15th December, the National Residential Landlords Association (NRLA) has raised concerns about how sensitive information will be handled and who may access it.

Data Protection Concerns for Landlords

The NRLA has written to the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) requesting confirmation that proper safeguards are in place before landlords are required to submit personal details. Key concerns focus on whether residential addresses and contact information could become publicly accessible, potentially creating security risks for property owners.

Particular attention has been drawn to landlords who may have experienced harassment, threats or domestic abuse. The association argues that inappropriate disclosure of home addresses could have serious consequences for these individuals. The NRLA is calling for publication of a completed Data Protection Impact Assessment before the register goes live.

Calls for Transparency and Safeguards

In its letter to the ICO, the NRLA has requested clear explanations about:

  • How landlord data will be stored and shared
  • Which parties will have access to sensitive information
  • What controls will govern use by letting agents and other authorised users
  • How long personal data will be retained

Ben Beadle, NRLA Chief Executive, stated: "Landlords face an impossible choice between complying with the law and protecting their personal safety if proper safeguards aren't confirmed. The government must clarify these details before expecting anyone to submit sensitive information."

Balancing Transparency With Privacy

While the register aims to improve transparency in the private rental sector, questions remain about how this will be balanced with individual privacy rights. The NRLA has suggested that if adequate protections cannot be guaranteed before December, the government should consider delaying implementation.

Property professionals may wish to monitor developments closely as the December rollout date approaches. The government has yet to respond to the NRLA's requests for clarification, leaving many landlords uncertain about what information they'll need to provide and how it will be protected.

As data-sharing initiatives continue to expand across the property sector, this situation highlights the ongoing challenge of reconciling regulatory transparency with robust personal data protection.

item.title: Huge fine for property firm after hundreds of complaints
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

A property sales firm has been ordered to pay over £277,000 in compensation to customers following an investigation by The Property Ombudsman (TPO). The firm, Let Property, faced nearly 200 complaints related to misrepresented rental income projections and unfair treatment of buyers. This marks the largest repayment of its kind, with average payments exceeding £3,200 per customer.

Let Property, which specialises in buy-to-let properties sold between landlords without evicting tenants, charged customers upfront fees of around £3,000 to reserve properties. However, many deals collapsed after valuations and rental income estimates were found to be misleading. TPO described the firm’s failings as “systemic,” prompting the substantial repayment order.

Customer Complaints and Systemic Issues

TPO’s investigation revealed that Let Property’s practices had caused significant financial harm to customers. Buyers were left out of pocket after deals fell through due to inaccurate information provided by the firm. The watchdog noted that the company’s shortcomings were widespread, affecting numerous transactions.

Let Property acknowledged that some customers had faced difficulties, particularly during completion processes in England. However, the firm disputed the total repayment figure quoted by TPO, stating that it had already paid £187,975 in awards to 63 individuals, including sellers, prospective landlords, and buyers. The company emphasised its commitment to improving services and ensuring fair treatment of customers.

Steps Towards Improvement

In response to the complaints, Let Property stated that it had introduced measures to enhance transparency and customer satisfaction. Since 2025, the firm has provided buyers with independent property condition assessments and pre-checks on rental income and tenancy agreements. Additionally, the company assigned dedicated sales progressors to guide buyers through the completion process, aiming to improve communication and support.

Despite these efforts, Let Property rejected claims of routine communication failures and defended its business model, asserting that it operates with fairness and transparency. The firm’s rapid growth—from one employee in 2022 to 57 last year—has raised questions about its ability to maintain service quality as it expands.

This case serves as a reminder for homeowners and landlords to exercise caution when engaging with property firms. Borrowers might consider seeking independent advice and verifying rental income projections before committing to buy-to-let investments. Whilst Let Property has pledged to address its shortcomings, this incident highlights the importance of due diligence in property transactions.

item.title: Limited companies outgrow individual BTL purchases for first time
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

For the first time on record, limited companies have overtaken individual landlords in buy-to-let property purchases, according to new research. Data from Paragon Bank reveals that 52% of mortgaged buy-to-let acquisitions in the first half of 2026 were made through limited companies – a dramatic shift from just 5% in 2018.

The rise of limited company BTL ownership

The trend towards company ownership has accelerated sharply in recent years. In 2022, limited companies accounted for 19% of purchases, rising to 25% in 2023, 34% in 2024 and 41% in 2025. The value of lending tells a similar story, with company purchases representing 53% of buy-to-let mortgage lending in early 2026 compared to just 6% eight years earlier.

HMRC figures obtained by Paragon through a Freedom of Information request show this pattern extends to property ownership more broadly. Non-individual purchasers now represent 42.1% of higher-rate additional dwelling Stamp Duty transactions, up from 15% in 2016/17. Over this period, transactions involving companies increased by 146%, while those by individuals fell by 41%.

Tax changes driving structural shift

This fundamental restructuring of the buy-to-let market stems largely from tax reforms introduced since 2015. The phased withdrawal of mortgage interest tax relief for individual landlords between 2017 and 2020 removed their ability to deduct finance costs from taxable rental income, replacing it with a basic-rate tax reduction.

The 2026 Budget added further momentum to this trend by announcing an additional four percentage point increase in tax rates on personally held property income from April 2027. With limited companies still able to claim mortgage interest as a business expense, the tax advantages of incorporation have become increasingly compelling.

Louisa Sedgwick, Paragon Bank's mortgages managing director, commented: "Limited company borrowing has moved from the margins to mainstream in under a decade. Government policy has been instrumental in this transformation, with landlords taking a more strategic, long-term approach to their investments."

For those considering buy-to-let investments, these figures highlight the growing importance of understanding different ownership structures. While incorporation brings potential tax benefits, it also involves additional administrative responsibilities and costs. Professional financial advice could help landlords evaluate the most suitable approach for their circumstances.

item.title: London rental competition eases as demand falls 31%
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The London rental market has seen a notable easing in competition, with tenant demand falling significantly in October after the peak summer season. According to recent data from Foxtons, registrations from prospective renters dropped by 31.2% between September and October, while the number of applicants per available property decreased from 20 to 14.

Seasonal Slowdown and Increased Supply

The decline in demand coincided with a slight rise in rental property availability, with new listings up by 2.8% compared to the same period last year. Average weekly rents also dipped by 4.8% month-on-month to £581, though Foxtons suggests this is largely due to seasonal trends rather than a structural market shift.

Year-to-date figures paint a mixed picture. While overall tenant registrations are down 10.4% compared to last year, certain areas like West London saw a 1.5% increase. Central London experienced the most significant decline at 15.3%. Despite lower demand, competition remains elevated, with an average of 17.7 prospective renters per property listing over the past year – 1.5% higher than in 2025.

Regional Variations in Rental Prices

Average rents across London have seen modest annual growth of 0.8%, reaching £589 per week. However, the figures vary considerably by location. Surrey led with a 9% increase, followed by North London at 5.4%. In contrast, East and West London saw declines of 0.9% and 1.8% respectively.

Budget-conscious renters may find some relief, with the average tenant spending 98% of their stated budget. Around 62% secured properties below their original price range, though 32% exceeded their planned expenditure. The typical rental budget now stands at £561 per week, up 1.1% year-on-year.

Sarah Tonkinson of Foxtons noted that while demand has softened in Central London, remaining applicants are offering higher budgets – up 4.1% compared to last year. She emphasised the importance of responsiveness in the current market, suggesting that landlords and agents who act quickly on enquiries could gain a competitive advantage during the quieter winter period.

As the market enters its seasonal lull, renters may find slightly more choice and potentially better negotiating power, particularly outside prime central locations. However, with long-term demand still outstripping supply in many areas, sustained rental growth could return in the new year.

item.title: Knight Frank cuts house price forecast to 1% for next year
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Leading property consultancy Knight Frank has significantly downgraded its UK house price forecasts, pointing to economic uncertainty and higher mortgage costs as key pressures on the market. The firm now expects average prices to rise just 1% in 2027, down from a previous prediction of 3% growth. Meanwhile, its five-year outlook to 2031 has been revised from 20.4% to 14.2%.

What's driving the slowdown?

Several factors are contributing to this more cautious outlook. Mortgage affordability remains stretched with five-year swap rates rising from 3.5% to 4.75% between late September and mid-November. Global geopolitical instability and domestic political uncertainty are also weighing on buyer confidence, according to Knight Frank's analysis.

Tom Bill, head of UK residential research at Knight Frank, noted: "The combination of higher borrowing costs alongside economic and political uncertainties continues to dampen market activity and price growth prospects."

Regional variations emerge

The forecast reveals striking regional disparities. Greater London is anticipated to underperform the national average due to longstanding affordability challenges. Prime central London faces particular headwinds, with prices now expected to fall 3% in 2027 compared to previous expectations of modest growth. item.title: Government’s EPC C target under pressure as landlords flag major obstacles
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

New research suggests England's private rental sector faces significant challenges in meeting the government's proposed energy efficiency targets, with nearly 2.5 million properties currently falling below the required standards. The findings from the TDS Charitable Foundation highlight multiple obstacles including unreliable EPC ratings, skills shortages and financial pressures that could hinder progress towards the 2030 deadline.

Landlords raise concerns over EPC reliability

The government's plan requires all privately rented homes in England to achieve at least an EPC C rating by 2030. However, the research reveals widespread scepticism about the current Energy Performance Certificate system, with many landlords questioning whether the ratings accurately reflect a property's true energy efficiency. Meanwhile, tenant awareness of EPCs remains surprisingly low, with some renters unaware of their property's rating or its significance.

These findings come as the EPC system prepares to take on greater importance in determining whether rental properties meet future legal standards. The TDS Charitable Foundation has called for earlier implementation of planned EPC reforms, currently not due until late 2027, to address these concerns and provide clearer guidance for landlords.

Practical barriers to energy efficiency improvements

Beyond questions about the EPC system itself, landlords report facing several practical challenges in upgrading properties:

  • A shortage of qualified tradespeople to carry out energy efficiency improvements
  • Concerns about the quality of available contractors and workmanship
  • Difficulty accessing clear information about government grants and support schemes
  • Financial pressures from rising improvement costs and potential rent increases

The research found particular confusion around available funding options, with both landlords and tenants struggling to navigate the various schemes and determine which might apply to their circumstances. Some landlords expressed frustration at the complexity of accessing financial support, while tenants worried that upgrade costs might ultimately be passed on through higher rents.

Calls for greater government support

In light of these findings, the TDS Charitable Foundation has urged ministers to consider additional measures to support the sector's transition, including:

  • Earlier implementation of EPC system reforms
  • More accessible financial support packages for landlords
  • Clearer guidance on available grants and funding options
  • Initiatives to address skills shortages in the retrofit sector

With the 2030 deadline approaching, these challenges raise important questions about whether the private rental sector can meet the government's energy efficiency ambitions without significant additional support. Property owners and tenants alike may wish to stay informed about potential changes to EPC requirements and available assistance as the policy develops.

item.title: London’s super-prime property sales slump as rival global markets surge
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

London's super-prime property market has seen a notable slowdown, with both transaction volumes and values declining in the third quarter of 2026. While the capital maintains its position among global luxury property hubs, recent data suggests buyers are turning their attention to rival markets in Asia and the Middle East.

Quarterly decline in London's luxury market

New research from Knight Frank reveals just 42 London homes sold for over $10m (£7.6m) between July and September 2026, down from 46 transactions in the previous quarter. The value of these deals fell more sharply, dropping 50% from $1.46bn to $722m quarter-on-quarter. Average transaction values nearly halved, falling from $31.7m to $17.2m.

Analysts suggest this reflects a temporary absence of exceptionally high-value deals rather than a fundamental market weakness. Whilst transaction numbers fell 9%, this represents a relatively modest decline compared to the value decrease. London now ranks sixth globally for both transaction numbers and total sales value among prime property markets.

Global super-prime hotspots outperform London

Dubai maintained its position as the world's busiest super-prime market with 86 sales, followed closely by Hong Kong (78) and New York (62). Sydney saw particularly strong growth, more than doubling its transactions to 57 and leapfrogging London in the rankings. Singapore also edged ahead with 44 deals.

Hong Kong surpassed Dubai in total transaction value for the first time since 2022, recording $1.58bn compared to Dubai's $1.57bn. The Asian financial hub saw transactions rise 39% year-on-year, with values up 52%. Meanwhile, Sydney's sales jumped 111% to a record 57 transactions, demonstrating the rapid growth of Australia's luxury market.

Longer-term perspective offers reassurance

Despite the quarterly dip, London's annual figures paint a more positive picture. The capital recorded 184 super-prime transactions in the year to September 2026, up from 173 during the whole of 2025. This suggests the market retains underlying strength despite facing increased competition globally.

Property experts note that London continues to outperform several major US markets, including Los Angeles which recorded just 18 super-prime sales - its lowest quarterly total. The capital's established legal system, cultural attractions and education system help maintain its appeal to international buyers, even as newer markets gain momentum.

While London's super-prime market faces challenges, its historic resilience and unique selling points suggest it may be experiencing a temporary adjustment rather than a sustained decline. Homeowners considering high-value property investments might wish to monitor how global economic conditions continue to reshape the luxury real estate landscape.

item.title: Rayner wants the interest earned from tenancy deposits
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The government has proposed new measures that would see a portion of interest earned on tenants' deposits redirected to the Treasury, in what could become a significant change for England's private rental sector. Housing Secretary Angela Rayner plans to give her department powers to collect earnings from custodial deposit schemes currently operated by three providers.

How deposit protection schemes currently work

Under existing rules in England, tenants' deposits must be protected in one of three government-approved schemes:

  • The Deposit Protection Service (DPS)
  • Tenancy Deposit Scheme (TDS)
  • MyDeposits

These schemes hold around £5.5bn in deposits collectively, with approximately half held in custodial arrangements where the scheme retains the deposit and any interest earned. Currently, this interest helps fund the free-to-use service for both landlords and tenants.

Proposed changes to deposit interest

The draft legislation, first reported by The Times, would allow the government to claim a share of this interest income from March 2027. While the exact percentage hasn't been specified, the rules aim to prevent scheme administrators from retaining "excessive" profits beyond what's needed to operate effectively.

The Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) states any revenue generated would be reinvested in tenant-focused programmes within the private rental sector. The proposals also include plans to phase out insured deposit schemes, where landlords currently hold deposits and keep the interest.

With approximately 4.7 million deposits protected across England and Wales, these changes could generate substantial income for the Treasury. However, the plans have drawn criticism from opposition parties, with the shadow housing secretary describing them as another form of "stealth tax".

Tenants and landlords in England may wish to monitor these developments, as the proposals could lead to changes in how deposit protection schemes operate. The government has confirmed it will publish regular updates about revenue collected under the new system once implemented.
